headline: ESBMC-ARDUINO: CLOSING THE DEPLOYMENT GAP FOR FORMAL VERIFICATION OF OPEN-HARDWARE PLCS
name: ESBMC-ARDUINO: CLOSING THE DEPLOYMENT GAP FOR FORMAL VERIFICATION OF OPEN-HARDWARE PLCS
description: scan-cycle model with idealized unbounded integers. The artifact that runs on the board, however, executes on a resource-constrained Microcontroller Unit (MCU) with a 16-bit machine word (8-bit AVR Arduinos), and sensors are read through a finite-resolution Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC). We show that this deployment gap makes naive width-aware verification unsound in practice: on 123 real third-party programs, checking 16-bit arithmetic overflow without a hardware input model raises a 44 % false-alarm rate (54/123) and finds zero genuine defects, because it explores sensor values no ADC can produce. Because the gap sits exactly where computation meets the physical process – a bounded sensor reading scaled by finite-width integer arithmetic into an actuation command – an overflow can silently suppress a physical safety action such as a high-level alarm. At the same time, an unbounded input model fabricates alarms that no environment can trigger. We present a method for hardware-faithful verification of IEC 61131-3 on open hardware: a declarative Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) descriptor (word width, ADC/Pulse-Width Modulation (PWM) resolution, I/O binding) and a sound lowering that interprets arithmetic at the target word width and constrains each input to its hardware-realizable range, transferring to the Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) domain the target-model discipline established for safety-critical embedded C (Frama-C, Astrée). We instantiate it for Arduino as ESBMC-Arduino, deriving HAL parameters from the official Arduino cores and realizing the input-range model as a lightweight hook in the Efficient SMT-based Context-Bounded Model Checker (ESBMC) Ladder Diagram (LD) frontend. On the 123-program corpus, the HAL annotator eliminates all 54 false alarms (54→0) while preserving every robustness proof, and a controlled corpus demonstrates the genuine – but rare – width-dependent defects the method detects with physically realizable witnesses.

hasPart.name: 1. Introduction
hasPart.description: Introduces the context of open-hardware PLCs and the problem of the deployment gap between abstract formal verification models and physical microcontroller execution constraints. It highlights the risks this gap poses to industrial control systems and outlines the motivation for the proposed research.

hasPart.name: 1.1 The Deployment Gap
hasPart.description: Discusses the specific discrepancies between ideal verification models, such as unbounded integer semantics, and actual MCU execution realities like finite bit-widths and ADC resolution limits.

hasPart.name: 1.2 Contributions
hasPart.description: Summarizes the core technical contributions of the paper, including hardware-faithful verification techniques and the evaluation of industrial open-hardware PLCs.

hasPart.name: 1.3 Scope
hasPart.description: Defines the operational boundaries and target environments covered by the proposed approach, focusing on Arduino-class devices and specific IEC 61131-3 languages.

hasPart.name: 2. Background
hasPart.description: Provides foundational background on programmable logic controllers, the PLC scan cycle, open-hardware toolchains, and bounded model checking principles.

hasPart.name: 2.1 The PLC Scan Cycle
hasPart.description: Explains the cyclic nature of PLC execution, detailing the phases of reading inputs, executing logic, and writing outputs.

hasPart.name: 2.2 Open-Hardware PLCs and the OpenPLC Toolchain
hasPart.description: Overview of open-hardware industrial controllers and how the OpenPLC ecosystem compiles IEC 61131-3 code into deployable binaries.

hasPart.name: 2.4 PLCopen XML
hasPart.description: Describes the XML-based standard format used to represent PLC programs, configurations, and function blocks across diverse engineering tools.

hasPart.name: 2.5 From PLCopen XML to a Binary: the OpenPLC Toolchain
hasPart.description: Details the compilation pipeline translating high-level PLCopen XML representations into executable C code and target-specific binaries.

hasPart.name: 2.6 Machine Models of Arduino-Class Targets
hasPart.description: Examines the hardware architectures and integer bit-width limitations characteristic of Arduino-class microcontrollers used in industrial settings.

hasPart.name: 2.7 Bounded Model Checking andk-Induction for PLCs
hasPart.description: Reviews formal verification techniques, specifically bounded model checking and k-induction, as applied to verifying safety properties in PLC programs.

hasPart.name: 3. Related Work
hasPart.description: Surveys existing literature and toolchains related to the formal verification of IEC 61131-3 programs and target-faithful analysis of embedded software.

hasPart.name: 3.1 Verification of IEC 61131-3
hasPart.description: Summarizes prior approaches and tools designed to check safety properties and functional correctness of programs written in IEC 61131-3 languages.

hasPart.name: 3.2 Target-Faithful Analysis of Embedded Software
hasPart.description: Discusses methods that account for underlying hardware characteristics during software analysis to prevent unsound verification results.

hasPart.name: 3.3 Code-Generation Correctness
hasPart.description: Reviews studies and verification techniques addressing bugs and discrepancies introduced during the automatic code generation and compilation process.

hasPart.name: 4. The Deployment Gap, Formally
hasPart.description: Formalizes the deployment gap mathematically, establishing the physical process, fault model, and motivating examples that demonstrate verification unsoundness.

hasPart.name: 4.1 Physical Process and Fault Model
hasPart.description: Outlines the physical process interactions and the specific fault model used to evaluate software anomalies caused by hardware constraints.

hasPart.name: 4.1.1 Fault model
hasPart.description: Details the types of hardware-induced faults considered, such as integer overflow behavior and quantization errors from analog inputs.

hasPart.name: 4.1.2 Assumptions
hasPart.description: States the formal assumptions regarding target execution environments, sensor characteristics, and environment behaviors.

hasPart.name: 4.1.3 Motivating example
hasPart.description: Presents a concrete programming example where abstract verification passes successfully while the physical implementation fails due to hardware constraints.

hasPart.name: 5. Hardware-Faithful Verification
hasPart.description: Introduces the core methodology for hardware-faithful verification, including the scan-cycle execution model, faithful lowering, and gap diagnosis.

hasPart.name: 5.1 Scan-Cycle Execution Model
hasPart.description: Formulates an accurate formal execution model that reflects how target microcontrollers handle the cyclic execution of PLC logic.

hasPart.name: 5.3 Faithful Lowering
hasPart.description: Describes the transformation process that maps high-level specifications down to bit-accurate representations matching the target hardware.

hasPart.name: 5.4 Soundness and Gap Diagnosis
hasPart.description: Proves the theoretical soundness of the proposed verification framework and explains how deployment gap discrepancies are diagnosed.

hasPart.name: 6.2 Implementation
hasPart.description: Details the practical implementation details of the verifier tool extension, focusing on integration hooks and configurability.

hasPart.name: 6.2.1 Where the Hook Sits
hasPart.description: Specifies the architectural placement of verification hooks within the compilation and analysis toolchain.

hasPart.name: 6.2.2 What the Hook Emits
hasPart.description: Explains the intermediate verification constraints and annotations emitted by the integration hook.

hasPart.name: 6.2.3 Configurability and Engineering
hasPart.description: Discusses engineering considerations and user-facing configuration options available in the implemented tool.

hasPart.name: 7. The Approach in Practice
hasPart.description: Demonstrates how the proposed hardware-faithful verification approach is applied from both an engineer's perspective and an internal architectural view.

hasPart.name: 7.1.1 Engineer’s View
hasPart.description: Illustrates the workflow and user experience for a control engineer using the hardware-faithful verification toolchain.

hasPart.name: 7.1.2 Under the Hood
hasPart.description: Provides a deep dive into the internal algorithms and translation mechanisms executing beneath the user interface.

hasPart.name: 8. Evaluation
hasPart.description: Presents experimental evaluation results addressing research questions regarding the frequency of the deployment gap, performance impacts, and soundness restoration.

hasPart.name: 8.1 Setup and Methodology
hasPart.description: Describes the experimental setup, benchmark suites, hardware targets, and metrics used to evaluate the verification approach.

hasPart.name: 8.2 RQ1: The Gap Is Real but Rare
hasPart.description: Evaluates how often deployment gaps occur in practice across real-world benchmark programs, finding them infrequent but critical when present.

hasPart.name: 8.3 RQ2: Naive Width-Aware Verification Is Unusable
hasPart.description: Analyzes the computational bottlenecks and scalability issues encountered when applying naive width-aware verification techniques.

hasPart.name: 8.4 RQ3: The HAL Annotator Restores Soundness
hasPart.description: Demonstrates that utilizing the hardware abstraction layer annotator effectively eliminates false negatives and restores verification soundness.

hasPart.name: 8.5 Cross-Tool Validation: the Gap Is Not Tool-Specific
hasPart.description: Compares results across multiple verification tools to confirm that the deployment gap is a fundamental hardware-software issue rather than an artifact of a single tool.

hasPart.name: 10. Threats to Validity
hasPart.description: Identifies potential internal and external validity threats to the experimental evaluation, including benchmark representativeness and tool assumptions.

hasPart.name: 11. Future Work
hasPart.description: Outlines promising future research directions, such as extending support to more complex microcontroller architectures and additional industrial protocols.

hasPart.name: 12. Conclusion
hasPart.description: Summarizes the main contributions of the paper, emphasizing the importance of hardware-faithful verification in closing the deployment gap for open-hardware PLCs.

hasPart.name: 8.6 RQ4: Performance and Completeness
hasPart.description: Evaluates the execution time, memory overhead, and completeness of the proposed hardware-faithful verification algorithm.

hasPart.name: 9. Discussion
hasPart.description: Reflects on the broader implications of the findings for industrial automation security, limitations of the current method, and broader impacts.
